JSON: Name: rumor_detection_microblogs Title: L1-regularized log-linear fusion of content, network, and platform-specific log-likelihood features for rumor retrieval and user belief classification in microblogs Short Hypothesis: Fusing content-based, network-based, and platform-specific log-likelihood ratio features using an L1-regularized log-linear model causes a statistically significant increase in mean average precision for rumor retrieval and F1 score for belief classification on annotated microblog datasets compared to regex-based retrieval and KL-divergence retrieval baselines. Related Work: Existing approaches address rumor and misinformation detection via three main strategies: (1) keyword- or regex-based retrieval to surface candidate posts, which attains high recall but yields many false positives; (2) language-model and retrieval-based ranking (e.g., KL-divergence with smoothing) that ranks candidate posts by text-model similarity but is sensitive to short-text sparsity and parameter choice; (3) meme- and network-oriented systems that exploit hashtags, URL propagation and re-tweet topology to detect coordinated or political memes. Prior belief- or stance-classification work relies on lexical sentiment features, dependency/sequence models, or thread-level context but typically targets overall sentiment rather than endorsement of specific unverified claims. Limitations across prior work include high false positive rates for broad queries, weak handling of microblog brevity and nonstandard language, limited use of combined user-history and URL content features, insufficient evaluation on large annotated rumor datasets, and poor cross-topic generalization when models are trained on narrow political or event-specific data. Abstract: This research addresses automated retrieval of rumor-related microblog posts and classification of user endorsement (belief) versus refutation or doubt. We propose a two-stage pipeline: construct per-feature probabilistic language models (content unigrams/bigrams, POS patterns, user posting and re-tweet histories, hashtags, and URL contents) and compute log-likelihood ratio scores for each tweet; then learn an L1-regularized log-linear model that linearly combines these feature-specific log-likelihood ratios to produce retrieval rankings and belief labels. The main contributions are (1) a feature-fusion formulation that treats each feature as a language model whose discriminative power can be combined via sparse weight learning, and (2) a reproducible experimental protocol for evaluating both retrieval (mean average precision) and belief classification (F1) on annotated rumor microblog data. Expected outcomes are substantial reductions in false positives for broad rumor queries and improved accuracy in identifying users who endorse versus question or deny rumors, enabling more reliable downstream misinformation analysis. Experiments: Datasets: annotated microblog dataset of ~10,000 tweets grouped into five rumor topics (example topics: obama_muslim, airfrance_photos, cellphone_numbers, michelle_staff, palin_divorce); each tweet labeled for rumor-relatedness and for belief class (endorse/deny/doubt/neutral). Data splits: per-topic 5-fold cross-validation and cross-topic holdout experiments (train on 4 topics, test on 1). Feature extraction: compute log-likelihood ratio features per tweet for TXT1 (unigram content), TXT2 (bigram content), POS1, POS2, USR1 (poster-history model), USR2 (re-tweeted-user-history model), TAG (hashtags), URL1 (unigram URL content), URL2 (bigram URL content). Retrieval evaluation: baselines = regex-based retrieval (original regex query), KL-divergence language-model ranking with Dirichlet smoothing (mu=2000 and mu tuned on train), random, and uniform majority-ranking. Metrics = Average Precision per topic, Mean Average Precision (MAP), precision@k (k=10,20), recall, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired significance tests (bootstrap or paired t-test) comparing MAPs. Retrieval setup: rank entire collected stream per topic using learned L1-regularized log-linear model (OWL-QN optimizer) applied to computed log-likelihood features; hyperparameter alpha grid search {0.001,0.01,0.1,1.0} on training folds. Ablation 1: evaluate retrieval performance using each feature group alone (content, network, twitter-specific) and cumulative addition. Ablation 2: leave-one-out feature ablation to quantify marginal contribution of each feature. Learning-curve experiment: vary number of labeled training tweets from 0 to 4000 in increments and report MAP and classification metrics. Belief classification evaluation: baselines = SVM (TF-IDF ngrams), logistic regression on raw n-grams, and majority class; metrics = accuracy, macro F1, precision, recall per class, Cohen's kappa; training uses class-weighted loss for imbalance. Cross-topic transfer: train fusion model on source topics, evaluate retrieval MAP and belief F1 on unseen target topic to quantify generalization. Report statistical significance where appropriate and provide per-topic confusion matrices and per-feature weight sparsity statistics. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Noisy short-text: extreme brevity, slang, misspellings and sarcasm in microblogs can degrade lexical and POS-based model quality; 2) Hashtag and URL sparsity: many tweets lack hashtags or external links, reducing signal for platform-specific features; 3) Incomplete user history: user-level features require sufficiently large historical data per account; sparse histories will weaken USR1/USR2 models and bias results toward active users; 4) URL content availability: relying on fetching external page content introduces failures when links are dead, shortened, rate-limited, or behind paywalls and can bias toward archival stability; 5) Annotation bias: labels depend on external rumor inventories and annotator judgment; class boundaries (doubt vs. deny) may be noisy and culturally dependent; 6) Class imbalance: endorsement vs. non-endorsement classes may be imbalanced, affecting classifier calibration and evaluation metrics; 7) Topic and temporal drift: models trained on past rumor instances may not generalize to novel rumors, different languages, or emergent events; 8) Scalability and compute: computing URL content models and per-user models at web scale incurs network and CPU costs and may not meet real-time constraints; 9) Ethical and privacy constraints: using user histories and external content may implicate privacy concerns and platform policy limitations, constraining data availability and reproducibility.
